Safety evaluation in sampling-based stochastic model predictive control often requires numerical estimation of exit functionals. This paper studies how existing higher-order methods for strong approximation of exit times can be brought into safe control. Two cases are highlighted. For general noncommutative dynamics, an adaptive order-1 Milstein discretization is used together with Lévy-area simulation via Wiktorsson's method. For commutative dynamics, an adaptive order-1.5 construction achieves a stronger exit-time rate. Under a local anti-concentration condition on the exit-time law, we show that strong exit-time approximation transfers to strong approximation of the failure indicator. The methods are then studied in the context of chance-constrained path integral control, which provides an exact continuous-time representation of safety through exit events. Numerical experiments compare the two cases in terms of strong exit-time error, failure-indicator error, and closed-loop constraint satisfaction, showing improvement over Euler-Maruyama and thereby enabling existing and future techniques whose applicability depends on improved strong approximation.

♻ ☆ Convergence of Sharpness-Aware Minimization Algorithms using Increasing Batch Size and Decaying Learning Rate
Hinata Harada, Hideaki Iiduka
The sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) algorithm and its variants, including gap guided SAM (GSAM), have been successful at improving the generalization capability of deep neural network models by finding flat local minima of the empirical loss in training. Meanwhile, it has been shown theoretically and practically that increasing the batch size or decaying the learning rate avoids sharp local minima of the empirical loss. In this paper, we consider the GSAM algorithm with increasing batch sizes or decaying learning rates, such as cosine annealing or linear learning rate, and theoretically show its convergence. Moreover, we numerically compare SAM (GSAM) with and without an increasing batch size and conclude that using an increasing batch size { achieves a lower worst-case $\ell_\infty$ adaptive sharpness} than compared with using a constant batch size and learning rate.

♻ ☆ On IDA-PBC with Maximum Energy Shapeability

Interconnection and Damping Assignment Passivity-Based Control (IDA-PBC) is a well-established stabilization technique for affine nonlinear systems. However, its application is generally hindered by the requirement of solving a set of partial differential equations (PDEs), i.e., the so-called matching equation. This paper explores the notion of maximum energy shapeability which describes the scenario that the homogeneous part of the matching equation admits $m$ independent solutions with $m$ the dimension of the control input. We show that the maximum energy shapeability enables a systematic procedure for the IDA-PBC design by transforming the matching equation into a set of new PDEs. Specifically, the transformed matching equation admits an explicit solution in the single input case. Sufficient conditions for maximum energy shapeability are also provided. It is shown that some existing constructive IDA-PBC designs actually implicitly exploit the maximum energy shapeability. The proposed procedure for the IDA-PBC design is demonstrated with two practical examples.

♻ ☆ Optimal Recursive Composition and Dyadic Phase Laws for Gradient Descent with Predetermined Stepsizes

Predetermined stepsize schedules featuring carefully chosen long steps have recently been shown to accelerate gradient descent (GD) on smooth convex functions. A prominent class of such schedules is built through recursive composition. In this paper, we characterize the convergence of these optimized recursive schedules, revealing a nonconstant log-periodic modulation across prescribed horizons. Specifically, we prove that for every $N \geq 1$, the optimized ConPP/OBS-S schedules satisfy $$f(x_{N-1})-f_\ast \le \frac{1}{2N^pΦ(\log_2N)-1} \frac{L}{2}\|x_0-x_\ast\|^2, \qquad p=\log_2(1+\sqrt2), $$ where $Φ$ is a positive, Lipschitz, nonconstant $1$-periodic function. We derive this by proving that balanced splitting is optimal at every horizon for these constructions, resolving a conjecture of Zhang and Jiang. Furthermore, for their asymmetric counterparts (ConPD/OBS-F schedules), we show that although optimal splits are not necessarily balanced, the same Silver exponent asymptotically persists alongside a distinct log-periodic modulation.

In reinforcement learning, more accurate policy evaluation has been frequently shown to improve downstream policy optimization performance. For tractability, most value estimators rely on $n$-step truncation and thereby omit the long-horizon behavior of the transition dynamics. Methods that instead capture this behavior through the global structure of the dynamics can converge faster, but their computational and memory requirements limit their scalability to large or continuous state spaces. To reconcile these limitations, we introduce Limiting-Kernel Q($λ$) (LKQL), an off-policy value estimator that uses the limiting kernel to approximate the long-horizon terms omitted by truncation. LKQL has the same order of complexity as $n$-step estimators and integrates directly into both on- and off-policy actor-critic algorithms. We prove that, under aperiodicity and in the near-on-policy regime, the operator underlying LKQL improves the policy evaluation convergence rate over its truncated counterpart for sufficiently large $n$, and that LKQL itself converges almost surely to the optimal values in finite Markov decision processes (MDPs) under a fixed behavior policy. On the MuJoCo continuous-control benchmark, we show that LKQL improves over $n$-step baselines in most settings, particularly on long-horizon tasks.

Shreve (SIAM Journal on Control and Optimization 22(6), pp. 856-877, 1984) with scalar mean-field interaction. Building on the prescribed performance control framework, a delay-dependent performance correction mechanism is introduced to ensure the boundedness of all signals in the closed-loop and to keep the output tracking error strictly within a dynamically adjusted performance envelope. This mechanism adapts in response to large delays that may cause performance degradation. In the absence of delays, the correction term vanishes, and the controller recovers the nominal (user-defined) performance envelope. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is validated through simulation studies.

In this paper, we introduce new CBO variants that address practical and theoretical limitations of the original formulation of this novel optimization methodology. First, we propose a model called $δ$-CBO}, which incorporates nonvanishing diffusion to prevent premature collapse to suboptimal states. We also develop a numerically stable implementation, the Consensus Freezing scheme, that remains robust even for arbitrarily large time steps by freezing the consensus point over time intervals. We connect these models through appropriate asymptotic limits. Furthermore, we derive from the Consensus Freezing scheme by suitable time rescaling and asymptotics a further algorithm, the Consensus Hopping scheme, which can be interpreted as a form of $(1,λ)$-Evolution Strategy. For all these schemes, we characterize for the first time the invariant measures and establish global convergence results, including exponential convergence rates.

Inverse Optimal Control (IOC) aims to infer the underlying cost functional of an agent from observations of its expert behavior. This paper studies the finite-horizon continuous-time inverse LQR problem from closed-loop state--input trajectories, where both the system matrices and the quadratic cost are unknown. The finite horizon induces a time-varying optimal gain, and this endogenous excitation serves as the structural mechanism that makes joint recovery possible. We quantify this mechanism through three computable conditioning indices, which measure state richness, gain-variation richness, and injectivity of a structured cost operator. Using these indices, we establish joint identifiability conditions for the inverse problem considered here. Crucially, these conditions guarantee recovery of the ground-truth system matrices $(A,B)$ and the true cost weighting matrices, rather than merely a behaviorally equivalent surrogate. We also develop a conditioning-aware sampled-data reconstruction method that reconstructs the gain $K(\cdot)$ and the closed-loop dynamics matrix $A_c(\cdot)$ from noisy measurements, recovers $(A,B)$ in closed form, and identifies the quadratic weights through a convex semidefinite program. We further establish the non-asymptotic perturbation bounds and the consistency of the full reconstruction method under sub-Gaussian observation noise, with explicit dependence on the same conditioning indices. Numerical experiments support the theory and illustrate the diagnostic value of the conditioning indices.

This paper aims to investigate the distributed stochastic optimization problems on compact embedded submanifolds (in the Euclidean space) where the local cost functions are weakly-convex. To address the manifold structure, we propose a distributed Riemannian stochastic proximal algorithm framework by utilizing the retraction and Riemannian consensus protocol, and analyze three specific algorithms: the distributed Riemannian stochastic subgradient, proximal point, and prox-linear algorithms. When the initial points satisfy certain conditions, we show that the iterates generated by this framework converge to a nearly stationary point in expectation while achieving consensus. We further establish the convergence rate of the algorithm framework as $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1+κ_g}{\sqrt{k}})$ where $k$ denotes the number of iterations and $κ_g$ shows the impact of manifold geometry on the algorithm performance. Finally, numerical experiments are implemented to demonstrate the theoretical results and show the empirical performance.

In this paper, we study the bias and high-order error bounds of the Linear Stochastic Approximation (LSA) algorithm with Polyak-Ruppert (PR) averaging under Markovian noise. We analyze the structure of the bias and show that the leading-order term is linear in $α$ and cannot be eliminated by PR averaging. To address this, we apply the Richardson-Romberg (RR) extrapolation procedure, which effectively cancels the leading bias term. We derive high-order moment bounds for the RR iterates and show that the leading error term aligns with the asymptotically optimal covariance matrix of the vanilla averaged LSA iterates.

♻ ☆ Convex Chance-Constrained Stochastic Control under Uncertain Specifications with Application to Learning-Based Hybrid Powertrain Control
Teruki Kato, Ryotaro Shima, Kenji Kashima
This paper proposes a strictly convex chance-constrained stochastic control framework that accounts for uncertainty in control specifications such as reference trajectories and operational constraints. Control inputs and risk allocation are jointly optimized under general, possibly non-Gaussian, uncertainties through sufficient deterministic conditions for probabilistic constraint satisfaction. A decreasing risk regularizer ensures existence and full use of the allowable risk. Under the stated regularity assumptions, the joint solution is unique and locally Lipschitz-continuous, supporting stable numerical optimization. The formulation is extended to learning-based exactly linearizable (EL) models through monotone state and input transformations. A hybrid powertrain example compares deterministic control, equal risk allocation, and optimized risk allocation with and without regularization in terms of charge sustaining, constraint violations, closed-loop cost, and solver time.
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Control Systems Technology (TCST)
♻ ☆ The First Step of Decision Making: Alignment under Semantic Uncertainty for Automated Operations Research
Chengxi She, Xingyu Lu, Yue Zhao, Qitao Shi, Caihua Chen
Problem definition: Automated operations research (OR) depends on correctly understanding the problem users intend to solve. In practice, limited user knowledge and vague expressions can obscure that problem, creating semantic uncertainty in the descriptions used for modeling. This uncertainty can lead to mathematical models that depart from users' intentions. We study semantic alignment to identify and correct errors or omissions in these descriptions before mathematical modeling. Methodology/results: We develop AMAO, an ambiguity-aware multi-agent framework for automated OR under semantic uncertainty. Its two-stage alignment process first uses semantic cues and contextual information to identify and correct potential semantic errors, then obtains additional information via human--AI interaction for further revision when the available context is insufficient. Specifically, AMAO integrates OR-guided mixture-of-experts (MoE) tuning and trajectory-based harness evolution to enhance semantic alignment capabilities. In addition, an ambiguity-aware benchmark and its matched multi-turn dialogue extension are proposed. Extensive experiments support that AMAO can recover the intended operational problem from ambiguous descriptions and recognize when available information is insufficient. Managerial implications: AMAO provides managers with an integrated workflow for translating ambiguous operational descriptions into mathematical models and optimization solutions. By combining semantic alignment with targeted user interaction, it supports recovery of the intended problem and improves downstream solution accuracy.
♻ ☆ On error bounds and noncritical Lagrange multipliers
Matúš Benko, Patrick Mehlitz
Critical Lagrange multipliers are known to be responsible for the potentially slow convergence of Newton-type methods, and noncriticality of a given multiplier has been tied to an error bound which estimates the distance of a primal-dual pair associated with a perturbed problem to the primal solution and the multiplier set of the unperturbed one, and is decisive for a local convergence analysis. We investigate this relation in an abstract setting where merely a set-valued mapping assigning primal-dual pairs to a parameter is available, and characterize the error bound of interest in terms of noncriticality of the underlying multiplier and two calmness-type properties of the associated multiplier mapping, one of which is a novel weak inner calmness in the fuzzy sense. No structural assumptions on the underlying problem are needed for that, and the two calmness-type conditions are not only sufficient but also necessary. Afterwards, we specify these findings for composite optimization problems. Whenever the subdifferential of the outer function is a polyhedral mapping, both conditions hold automatically, which explains the equivalence of noncriticality and the error bound observed in the polyhedral setting. Whenever the outer function is $C^2$-decomposable, they are secured by calmness of a restricted multiplier mapping together with a closedness condition, which recovers and extends the known characterization for $C^2$-cone reducible constraint systems.

♻ ☆ Exact Verification of First-Order Methods via Mixed-Integer Linear Programming
Vinit Ranjan, Jisun Park, Stefano Gualandi, Andrea Lodi, Bartolomeo Stellato
We present exact mixed-integer linear programming formulations for verifying the performance of first-order methods for parametric quadratic optimization. We formulate the verification problem as a mixed-integer linear program where the objective is to maximize the infinity norm of the fixed-point residual after a given number of iterations. Our approach captures a wide range of gradient, projection, proximal iterations through affine or piecewise affine constraints. We derive tight polyhedral convex hull formulations of the constraints representing the algorithm iterations. To improve the scalability, we develop a custom bound tightening technique combining interval propagation, operator theory, and optimization-based bound tightening. Numerical examples, including linear and quadratic programs from network optimization, sparse coding using Lasso, and optimal control, show that our method provides several orders of magnitude reductions in the worst-case fixed-point residuals, closely matching the true worst-case performance.
♻ ☆ A restart-free accelerated algorithm for nonconvex minimization: continuous- and discrete-time analysis
Kansei Ushiyama, Shun Sato
We propose two deterministic momentum-based first-order methods for minimizing lower-bounded nonconvex functions with Lipschitz-continuous gradients and Hessians. Both methods attain an $\varepsilon$-approximate first-order stationary point in $O(\varepsilon^{-7/4})$ function and gradient evaluations, and their update parameters do not depend on the target accuracy or a prescribed terminal iteration. The convergence guarantees concern the best point among weighted averages of the iterates. Instead of relying on momentum-resetting restarts, both methods employ a velocity-control mechanism that adaptively reduces the velocity. The first method uses a differentiable velocity-control rule, making its last iterate differentiable with respect to the initial point. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first deterministic first-order method to combine this differentiability property with the stated complexity. The second method adaptively estimates the gradient and Hessian Lipschitz constants and requires no prior knowledge of their values. Numerical experiments show that it outperforms existing parameter-free methods on some test problems. Both methods are derived by discretizing a new continuous-time model described by an ordinary differential equation. We develop parallel continuous- and discrete-time convergence analyses within the performance estimation problem framework.
♻ ☆ Optimal Diagonal Preconditioning Beyond Worst-Case Conditioning: Theory and Practice of Omega Scaling
Saeed Ghadimi, Woosuk L. Jung, Arnesh Sujanani, David Torregrosa-Belén, Henry Wolkowicz
We study optimal diagonal preconditioning using the classical worst-case $κ$-condition number and the averaging-based $ω$-condition number. For the $κ$-optimal preconditioning problem, we derive an affine-based pseudoconvex reformulation with three key advantages: all stationary points are global minima, subgradients are inexpensive to compute, and the optimization variable is an $n$-dimensional vector rather than an $n\times n$ matrix as in semidefinite programming (SDP) approaches. We develop a simple and highly efficient subgradient method, with convergence guarantees, for solving this pseudoconvex formulation that is substantially more scalable and accurate than existing SDP-based methods. For the $ω$-condition number, we provide explicit characterizations of optimal diagonal and block diagonal preconditioners. In particular, we show that several classical preconditioners, including Jacobi and row/column normalization, are $ω$-optimal, and that matrix balancing schemes monotonically reduce $ω$ and converge to stationary points of the two-sided problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first unified and explicit characterization of optimality conditions for both $κ$ and $ω$-based preconditioning. Our numerical experiments further reveal a striking phenomenon: although $κ$-optimal preconditioners achieve stronger reductions in the worst-case condition number, $ω$-optimal preconditioners are substantially cheaper to compute and yield better performance for iterative methods such as preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) and least squares method (LSQR). Moreover, applying $ω$-optimal scaling to linear systems that are already $κ$-optimally preconditioned leads to further improvements in PCG iterations.
♻ ☆ A Backend-Agnostic MWIS Kernel for Stochastic Unit Commitment with Neutral-Atom Hardware Validation
Jiying Chen, Min Lin, Jingwei Wen, Zhihong Zhang, Chuixiong Wu
Quantum hardware is beginning to address structured combinatorial optimisation, but two steps still block practical use: mapping real operational models onto hardware-compatible instances, and converting noisy hardware output back into feasible decisions. Here we introduce a backend-agnostic computational interface that compiles the discrete decision layer of stochastic unit commitment into a move-based maximum-weight independent set (MWIS) problem, while retaining continuous dispatch and feasibility recovery in the classical computational layer. We validate the approach in a green hydrogen scheduling setting and deploy it on the QuEra Aquila neutral-atom quantum processor. This is the first end-to-end industrial scheduling workflow that connects real operational decisions to programmable neutral-atom hardware through a solver-agnostic MWIS representation. Across a 15-day hardware campaign on 50-node instances, hardware-generated solutions after classical refinement match or exceed the dispatch margins obtained from exact MWIS on every day. When scaling to 144 nodes, encoding quality remains stable, while the probability that the full atom array survives, rather than graph embedding, emerges as the dominant bottleneck to further scaling. Together, these results establish a hardware-compatible computational pathway toward larger problem scales, and lay the groundwork for exploring regimes in which exact classical optimisation may no longer scale efficiently.

♻ ☆ Sequential Conformal Calibration under Recursive Selection
Yuning Yang, Zexuan Liu, Tianci Wang, Danlin Li
Conformal prediction provides finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees that can support decision-making in specific settings. In multistage problems, earlier decisions determine the populations relevant to later calibration. When later scores are refit using earlier calibration results, reusing those cases for ranking need not preserve exchangeability with a surviving test case. We study sequential conformal calibration with a fresh fold at each stage: conditional on earlier folds, the selected fold scores and the surviving test score are exchangeable. This yields finite-sample coverage guarantees for every prefix of the decision sequence. For atomless survivor score distributions, we derive a universal Binomial-thinned Beta chain for the realized coverage process. Its law depends only on fold sizes and target levels, even under predictable refitting, and yields exact coverage slack, abstention probabilities, and calibration-conditional guarantees. We further characterize the tradeoff between freshness and data reuse. For fixed scores, strict-survivor reuse is exactly valid. For adaptive scores refit using past calibration data, reusing survivors can incur worst-case rank loss, while blocked designs provide an intermediate option between full reuse and stagewise fresh folds. As a case study, we apply the framework to serial multi-echelon inventory problem and propose a sequential conditional-quantile formulation. Each stock level is learned as a context-dependent quantile of cumulative demand among scenarios satisfying earlier no-backlog constraints. We connect these targets to common-shift stationarity and derive decision-level implications for the resulting calibrated policies. In a three-echelon simulation, fresh-fold refitting achieves 81.98% final-prefix coverage against an 81.82% target while reducing mean cost by 5.5% relative to the Bonferroni baseline.

♻ ☆ ReLoop: Structured Modeling and Behavioral Verification for Reliable LLM-Based Optimization
Junbo Jacob Lian, Yujun Sun, Huiling Chen, Chaoyu Zhang, Hanzhang Qin, Chung-Piaw Teo
Large language models (LLMs) can translate natural-language problem descriptions into optimization code, but the code is prone to silent failures: it executes and returns a solver-feasible solution while encoding a semantically incorrect formulation. On compositional problems, the resulting feasibility-correctness gap reaches 90 percentage points. We introduce ReLoop, which combines two mechanisms. Structured generation decomposes code production into a four-stage reasoning chain (understand, formalize, synthesize, verify) to reduce formulation errors during generation. Behavioral verification detects the errors that remain by testing whether the formulation responds correctly to solver-based parameter perturbation, a signal that comes from the solver rather than from LLM self-review and requires no ground truth. The two mechanisms address different error structures: structured generation gives the largest gain on compositional problems (+8.5pp accuracy on RetailOpt-190 with Claude Opus 4.6), and behavioral verification gives its largest gain on localized defects (+4.4pp on MAMO-ComplexLP). With diagnostic execution recovery, ReLoop reaches 100% executable code on Claude Opus 4.6, and relative to direct generation it raises or preserves every reported metric of the three chat-tuned foundation models on all three benchmarks. For the narrowly fine-tuned SFT model we test, the chain-of-thought prompt conflicts with its learned output format and lowers its accuracy on MAMO-ComplexLP; we document and analyze this interaction. We release RetailOpt-190, 190 compositional retail optimization scenarios in which several constraints interact.

♻ ☆ Single-Loop Stochastic Projected Damped Extragradient Methods for Nonconvex--(Strongly) Concave Minimax Optimization
Huiling Zhang, Minhao Zhang, Zi Xu, Yuhong Dai
We develop single-loop stochastic projected damped extragradient methods for nonconvex--(strongly) concave minimax optimization, with complexity guarantees for both game stationarity (GS) and optimization stationarity (OS). Our approach combines a stochastic projected damped extragradient (SPDE) method with a recursive variance-reduced variant, VR-SPDE, both of which retain a single-loop structure. Under an unbiased stochastic gradient oracle with uniformly bounded variance, SPDE finds an $\varepsilon$-game-stationary point with stochastic first-order oracle (SFO) complexities of $O(κ\varepsilon^{-4})$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-5})$ in the nonconvex--strongly concave and nonconvex--concave settings, respectively, where $κ=L/μ$. Under an additional mean-square Lipschitz condition on the stochastic gradients, VR-SPDE improves these GS complexities to $O(κ^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3})$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-9/2})$, respectively. For an $\varepsilon$-optimization-stationary point, SPDE achieves SFO complexities of $O(κ\varepsilon^{-4})$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-6})$, while VR-SPDE achieves $O(κ^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3})$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-6})$, in the two settings, respectively. These OS guarantees match the best-known bounds achieved by multi-loop methods while preserving a single-loop implementation. To the best of our knowledge, our results provide the best-known SFO complexity guarantees among single-loop stochastic first-order methods for the respective stationarity criteria and problem classes.
♻ ☆ Practical Regularized Quasi-Newton Methods with Inexact Function Values
Hiroki Hamaguchi, Naoki Marumo, Akiko Takeda
Many practical optimization problems involve objective function values that are corrupted by unavoidable numerical errors. In smooth nonconvex optimization, quasi-Newton methods combined with line search are widely used due to their efficiency and scalability. These methods implicitly assume accurate function evaluations and thus may fail to converge in noisy settings. Developing fast and stable quasi-Newton methods for such scenarios is therefore crucial. To address this issue, we propose a novel noise-tolerant regularized quasi-Newton method equipped with a relaxed Armijo-type line search, designed to remain stable under inaccurate function evaluations. By combining a regularization parameter update rule inspired by Objective-Function-Free Optimization and the AdaGrad-Norm method, we prove an order-optimal $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ complexity bound under errors in function values. We performed extensive experiments on the CUTEst benchmark collection with artificially noisy objective function evaluations, as well as with low-precision floating-point arithmetic (64-, 32-, and 16-bit). The results demonstrate stable performance under reduced precision and function-value noise while retaining practical convergence speed and computational cost.

☆ Nonlinear Feedback Control in High Dimensions using the Polynomial-Polynomial Regulator
Nicholas A. Corbin, Boris Kramer
We consider the problem of computing Taylor approximations to the optimal feedback law and value function for infinite-horizon finite-dimensional nonlinear optimal control problem---also known as Al'brekht's method. The scalability of existing Al'brekht-based approaches to computing approximate solutions to the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation associated with the optimal control problem has been severely limited by computational resources. The computational time issue has been partially mitigated by recent works leveraging tensor-structure to develop efficient numerical methods. However, RAM requirements still have remained a major hindrance to scaling beyond state dimensions of a few hundred or low thousands. We propose an acceleration to compute the expensive higher-order terms in a reduced space, mitigating the curse of dimensionality. A fast and scalable \textsc{Matlab} implementation is provided open-source for general purpose use, with the ability to accommodate arbitrary polynomial nonlinearities in the control-affine state equation, as well as polynomial state-dependence in the cost function, and the ability to handle systems in generalized form with a non-identity mass matrix, such as finite element models. Combined with the exploitation of sparsity and modern low-rank Riccati solvers, this permits computing approximations to polynomial feedback laws based on Al'brekht's method in hundreds of thousands of states.

☆ An Efficient, Lean 4 Verified Necessary and Sufficient Condition for Membership in Pedigree Polytopes
T. S. Arthanari
The set \(P_{n}\) consists of the characteristic vectors of pedigrees, which are combinatorial encodings in one-to-one correspondence with Hamiltonian cycles. For \(n \geq 4\) and \(τ_{n} = \binom{n}{3}-1\), the Membership Problem for the Pedigree Polytope (M3P) asks whether a given vector \(X \in \mathbb{Q}^{τ_{n}}\) belongs to \(\mathrm{conv}(P_n)\). This paper gives a complete account, with the full proof statements and machine-verified Lean~4 certificates, of the necessary and sufficient (\NS) condition established in Chapter~5 of \emph{Pedigree Polytopes: New Insights on Computational Complexity of Combinatorial Optimisation Problems} (Arthanari, 2023): membership of $X$ in $\mathrm{conv}(P_n)$ is characterised by the feasibility, at every stage $k=4,\dots,n-1$, of a recursively constructed layered network, together with, when needed, a multicommodity flow problem $\mathrm{MCF}(k-1)$ achieving its maximum possible flow $z_{\max}$. We present the construction, the \NS{} condition itself, and the proofs of this characterisation, together with the resulting polynomial-time algorithm for M3P. Both directions of the \NS{} condition --- sufficiency and necessity (the multicommodity-flow feasibility argument of the book's Chapter~5) --- are machine-verified in Lean~4/Mathlib4 with zero unresolved \texttt{sorry}s in either dependency chain. The \NS{} characterisation therefore follows directly from the two machine-checked implications. The complete Lean~4 project is publicly available. A companion introductory article (arXiv:2507.09069) presents the same material for a broader readership, without the Lean~4 verification; the present paper adds full statements, proof sketches, and the complete machine-checked certificates.

☆ Two Linear Programs are Better than One
Alexander E. Black, Christoph Hertrich, Stefan Kober, Georg Loho
The extension complexity $\operatorname{xc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$ is the minimum number of facets of a polytope that projects onto it. Motivated by the complexity of neural networks, Hertrich and Loho introduced the virtual extension complexity $\operatorname{vxc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$, which is the minimum of $\operatorname{xc}(Q) + \operatorname{xc}(R)$ among all polytopes $Q$ and $R$ such that $P+Q=R$. We show the following results pertaining to virtual extension complexity. First, we resolve the core open problem on the topic by showing the virtual extension complexity can be exponentially smaller than extension complexity. Second, we show there are matroid base polytopes with exponential virtual extension complexity by adapting a semi-algebraic counting argument by Hrubeš that extends the counting arguments of Rothvoss. Finally, we show that the maximum virtual extension complexity of a polygon with $n$ vertices is $Θ(\sqrt{n})$. This resolves an analogue of a question on extension complexity of Fiorini, Rothvoss, and Tiwary in 2011 in the case of virtual extension complexity.
☆ The $p$-Bures-Wasserstein distance via $3\times3$ block matrices (with application to $p$-Bures-Wasserstein barycenters)
Suvrit Sra
We study the $p$-Bures-Wasserstein distance $D_p(A,B)=(\mathrm{tr}\,A^p+\mathrm{tr}\,B^p-2\|A^{1/2}B^{1/2}\|_p^p)^{1/2}$ on positive semidefinite matrices; it equals the Bures-Wasserstein distance for $p=1$, and the Hilbert-Schmidt distance for $p=2$. We prove that $D_p$ is a metric for every $1\le p\le2$, by proving a stronger 2014 conjecture of Lin and van den Driessche on $3\times3$ block matrices. Our main tool is a partition inequality for Schatten norms, proved by complex interpolation. We also characterize Fréchet means for $D_p$ by a fixed-point equation and prove geometric convergence of the associated iteration.

☆ Entropy-Regularized Mean-Field Games with Average-Reward Criterion: Span-Seminorm Contractions and Model-Free Learning
Gunes Akbas, Naci Saldi, Berkay Anahtarci, Can Deha Kariksiz
We study stationary discrete-time mean-field games with finite state and action spaces under the average-reward criterion, with an entropy-regularized objective and population-dependent dynamics and rewards. Under a minorization condition, the soft Q-operator is a span-seminorm contraction for the full transition kernel, so relative value iteration does not require the minorizing measure. When the Lipschitz constant of the kernel is below the minorization mass and the temperature exceeds an explicit threshold, the equilibrium fixed-point operator is a contraction: an equilibrium exists, its population distribution is unique, and a fixed-point iteration converges to it geometrically. We then learn the equilibrium model-free from a simulator, combining soft Q-learning at a fixed population distribution with an empirical transition kernel. We prove a finite-sample bound for soft Q-learning in the span seminorm, with temperature-independent constants, and derive convergence rates for the learned population distribution and policy. A congestion-aware routing game illustrates the results.

☆ Quantum ordinal optimization under a fixed comparison budget
Hongyu Wu
Ordinal optimization selects designs that are good enough rather than optimal when evaluation is expensive and the budget is small. The alignment probability measures the chance that the selected set contains at least a prescribed number of truly good designs. We formulate quantum ordinal optimization as a class of problems that maximize this probability under a fixed oracle budget. We study exact, coherent pairwise comparisons with one selected design as a first instance, with the budget counted in comparison queries. For every classical comparison budget smaller than the number of designs, we prove that a knockout among uniformly sampled designs attains the optimum. The sample is drawn without replacement and contains one more design than the number of comparisons. For a uniformly random order, the selected design's rank has a polynomial probability law. At the same comparison budget, the maximum quantum degree is at most twice the classical maximum, a factor attained whenever there are more than twice as many designs as comparisons, so a quantum algorithm can realize rank laws that no classical algorithm with the same budget can. We determine the exact quantum optimum with one comparison for every number of designs and every good-enough set. For selecting the best of n designs, the optimal success probability with one quantum comparison is approximately 3.30/n for large n, compared with 2/n for one classical comparison. When the best design is sought, one quantum comparison gives a higher alignment probability than two classical comparisons whenever there are more than nine designs.

☆ Homogenization of an optimal control problem for a Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system in a 3D perforated domain
Amartya Chakrabortty, Haradhan Dutta, Hari Shankar Mahato
We study the homogenization of an optimal control problem governed by a Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system in a periodically perforated three-dimensional domain. The obstacles are Lipschitz sets of size $\varepsilon^α$, $α>3$, where $\varepsilon$ is the period. The fluid satisfies the no-slip condition on the outer boundary and the free-slip condition on the obstacles, the phase-field equation contains a source term, and the convective term carries a pore-scale Reynolds number that tends to zero as $\varepsilon\to0$. The control is a distributed body force, and the cost functional tracks the velocity in $L^2$ and the order parameter in $H^1$. Since uniqueness of weak solutions of the state system is not known for fixed $\varepsilon$, the control-to-state relation is multivalued, and we pose the microscopic problems over control-state pairs. We prove the existence of microscopic optimal pairs and the sequential $Γ$-convergence of the cost functionals to the cost functional of a control problem governed by the unsteady Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system on the full domain. As a consequence, the optimal values converge, every cluster point of microscopic optimal pairs is optimal for the homogenized problem, and the optimal controls converge strongly along the corresponding subsequences. The $\liminf$ inequality follows from the homogenization of the state system, including the strong convergence of the gradients of the order parameter. Only the recovery sequence requires uniqueness of weak solutions of the homogenized system, which we prove when the outer boundary is of class $C^{2,1}$.

☆ KKT Residual Sliding Manifolds: A Projection-Free Structured Finite-Time Solver for Nonlinear Constrained Optimisation
Abdelhafid Zenati, Kamal Youcef-Toumi
Nonlinear Constrained Optimisation (NCO) requires simultaneous satisfaction of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions. Existing methods enforce these conditions through projections, penalties, barriers, or sequential approximations, potentially introducing computational complexity and convergence difficulties. For nonconvex problems, a KKT point need not be a local optimum. This paper reformulates NCO as stabilisation of a unified KKT sliding residual manifold and develops SM-KKT, a projection-free solver. Stationarity, equality feasibility, and regularised Fischer-Burmeister complementarity are integrated into a unified residual system, with complementarity encoding inequality feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness. The manifold's zero set is shown to be equivalent to the KKT conditions. The required Jacobian saddle-point inertia is characterised and shown, under stated assumptions, to be equivalent to the simultaneous satisfaction of the Linear Independence Constraint Qualification (LICQ) and Second-Order Sufficient Condition (SOSC). This characterisation establishes local stability of the structured correction algorithm under these conditions and distinguishes nondegenerate locally optimal KKT solutions from points failing second-order optimality. SM-KKT computes structured primal--dual corrections and applies a discrete sliding reaching law to drive the KKT residual into a prescribed boundary layer in finite time. Four nonlinear benchmarks show recovery of reference constrained optima with KKT residuals below $10^{-6}$, earlier boundary-layer reaching, and favourable KKT accuracy compared with projected primal-dual, augmented-Lagrangian, quadratic-penalty, and log-barrier baselines.
☆ Beyond Aggregate Drift: Optimal Client-Specific Windows in Federated Learning
Yuriy Dorn, Dmitrii Vishovan, Kirill Novoselov, Ilya Kuruzov, Darina Dvinskikh, Alexander Gasnikov
We study federated learning from continuously arriving data: each client samples from its own distribution, these distributions drift over time, and the server must track the minimizer of the clients' weighted average loss. Clients are not alike as they collect data at different rates, with different noise, and change at different speeds. The main question is how much history should each one keep? A single shared window must serve every client at once, and so makes a fast-changing client carry the sampling noise of a slow, nearly stationary one. We give each client a memory of its own, sized to that client's noise, arrival rate, and drift, and refresh it by restarted accelerated method that starts from a common point. The tracking error is then bounded by \[ R\left(\sum_m w_m^{3/2}\,σ_m\sqrt{γ_m/λ_m}\right)^{2/3}, \] for clients with weight $w_m$, noise $σ_m$, arrival rate $λ_m$, and drift rate $γ_m$ on a domain of diameter $R$. This is never worse than what any common window can achieve, and strictly better whenever noise and drift are spread unevenly across clients. A lower bound that puts different groups of clients on different drift clocks shows this quantity is the right one. The two bounds agree up to a constant whenever the clients occupy boundedly many refresh scales, and in general differ only by the sixth root of the number of scales. Experiments show the gain comes from the memory rather than from the solver: it persists across accelerated, stochastic-gradient, and one-step methods, and against a separately tuned common-memory baseline.

Non-firm connection products can accelerate grid access while reinforcements are delayed, but their planning value depends on evidence supporting the contractual promise. Stage C treats the resulting ledger as fixed in queue-aware allocation and intervention planning. In the primary policy-package evaluation, the evidence-supported menu returns the same $2.119$~GW allocation as firm-only access, whereas authorizing the uniformly derated fallback raises awards to $6.442$~GW and reduces backlog from $136.076$ to $113.601$~GW-years; all $4.489$~GW of non-firm awards use the fallback. In a target-free matched control, evidence-routed and state-blind fallback menus attain primary objectives equivalent within EUR~1 and return the same accepted applicants, award years, routes, and intervention portfolio. Thus, in the reported testbed, fallback authorization rather than calendar-specific evidence support drives the access-volume effect.

We completely classify cyclic steepest descent (CSD) on strictly convex quadratics whose Hessian has exactly two distinct eigenvalues. For every $m\ge2$, write $A=aP+bQ$ with $00$ is precisely the nonterminating exceptional set: there the convergence is $R$-linear with factor $(b-a)/(b+a)$, whereas every other nonterminating initialization is $R$-superlinear and one-eigenspace initializations terminate in one step. The exceptional cone has Lebesgue measure zero, so $R$-superlinear convergence holds almost everywhere in this two-spectrum class. The main results of this paper were obtained through a generative-AI workflow using OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol, Anthropic Claude Fable 5, and OpenAI GPT-6 Astra. Further details appear in the disclosure at the end of the paper.

☆ Explicit Bounds on Hoffman Constants for Sparse Polyhedral Regularizers
Faris Chaudhry, Anthea Monod, Keisuke Yano
Hoffman constants quantify the distance to the solution set of a polyhedral system in terms of its residual; they control error bounds, geometric conditioning, the convergence rate of first-order iterative algorithms, and the stability of regression estimators to target perturbations. Despite their importance, explicit values of Hoffman constants are rarely available due to their computational complexity. In this paper, we derive explicit bounds on the Hoffman constant for a class of structured polyhedral systems arising in sparse regularization. We show that the constants admit a decomposition into spectral, geometric, and interaction components, which together determine their scaling behavior. This framework explains the gap between worst-case dimension-dependent bounds and the favorable conditioning observed empirically in structured problems. As a primary application, we analyze $\ell_1$-regularized least squares, demonstrating that the effective constants depend on low-dimensional active subspaces rather than the ambient dimension. We then extend to the elastic net and adaptive $\ell_1$-regularized formulations, demonstrating how the underlying optimization geometry is altered by the $\ell_2$ penalty and reweighting scheme. Furthermore, we relate our results to classical statistical assumptions and show that the restricted eigenvalue condition bounds only the primal curvature of the active set, leaving the dual interaction geometry unconstrained and is thus insufficient alone for fast theoretical convergence rates. We further show standard $\ell_\infty$ coherence conditions do not yield dimension-independent Euclidean bounds to close this gap. Our theoretical results show that Hoffman constants admit explicit, interpretable forms in structured regression settings and, in practice, provide actionable tools for post-hoc feature pruning and a priori optimal hyperparameter selection.

♻ ☆ Comparing Socially-Equitable Renewable Energy Budget Allocation MDP Policies in Mature and Emerging Economies
Riya Kinnarkar, Mansur M. Arief, Yan Pratama Akhra, Dino Arla
Equitable renewable-energy planning is a sequential decision problem, but the decision variables available to a public planner differ sharply between mature and emerging economies. In the former the government largely builds generation, while in the latter it steers private investment through incentives and quotas. We formulate socially-equitable renewable-energy budget allocation as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and, using a single problem-agnostic solver interface, compare the same policies across the two settings: eight U.S. cities (a mature economy) and West Java, Indonesia (an emerging economy). The results show that across both settings, a receding-horizon value-iteration policy dominates. In the U.S., it reaches 66% renewable penetration while cutting the underserved low-income population by 96% versus a random baseline. In West Java it closes the low-access gap while crowding in about seven times the private capital of a naive market-chasing heuristic. More interestingly, this heuristic, which is mildly sub-optimal in the U.S., could yield catastrophic outcomes in Indonesia, by underserving every low-access region, because chasing attractive markets and serving the underserved diverge once the planner acts through private developers.
♻ ☆ Tight Complexity of Muon under Heavy-Tailed Noise
Jiayu Zhang, Tianyi Lin
A growing lesson from neural network optimization is that optimizer design should respect how the model is parametrized. The layerwise input-output structure of neural networks motivates Muon and Scion, whose updates also support hyperparameter transfer. At the same time, stochastic gradient noise in deep learning is often far from sub-Gaussian and may exhibit heavy tails. These observations have shaped recent algorithmic principles for training neural networks, yet their joint theoretical consequences are underexplored. In particular, it is unclear what dimension dependence is unavoidable for gradient-based methods when the problem class is defined using an input-output norm and the stochastic gradient noise is heavy-tailed, and if higher-order smoothness can accelerate optimization. We study these questions through nonconvex smooth stochastic optimization over $\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ equipped with general norms and under $p^\mathrm{th}$-moment heavy-tailed noise, where the goal is to achieve an $ε$-stationary point in the dual norm. Our first contribution is a dimension-dependent lower bound: when $\max\{m,n\}$ is large enough, any method using only the stochastic gradients requires $Ω(\min\{m, n\}ε^{-\frac{3p-2}{p-1}})$ oracle calls for the problem class defined by the spectral norm, which is a common input-output matrix norm. We prove that a batched Muon method with the spectral norm can achieve the matching upper bound of $O(\min\{m, n\}ε^{-\frac{3p-2}{p-1}})$. To exploit higher-order smoothness, we propose a transported Muon method and improve the bound to $O(\min\{m, n\}ε^{-\frac{5p-3}{2p-2}})$ when the norm is spectral and the Hessian is Lipschitz. Finally, we incorporate practical heuristics into our transported method and evaluate it across multiple architectures and model sizes, showing its compatibility with neural network training.

♻ ☆ On the Convergence of Constrained Gradient Method
Danqing Zhou, Hongmei Chen, Shiqian Ma, Junfeng Yang
The constrained gradient method (CGM) has recently been proposed to solve convex optimization and monotone variational inequality (VI) problems with general functional constraints. While existing literature has established convergence results for CGM, the assumptions employed therein are quite restrictive; in some cases, certain assumptions are mutually inconsistent, leading to gaps in the underlying analysis. This paper derives rigorous and improved convergence guarantees for CGM under weaker and more reasonable assumptions, covering strongly convex optimization problems, as well as VI problems under both strongly monotone and general monotone settings. Preliminary numerical experiments are provided to verify the validity of CGM and demonstrate its efficacy in addressing such problems.
♻ ☆ Cosm: orchestrated collective dynamics give rise to rapid computational search at the solution frontier
Kenneth M. Zick, Nikhil Shukla, Alexander Marakov
We introduce Collective Switched Motion (Cosm), a heuristic optimization framework based on orchestrated collective dynamics. Cosm organizes the objective into conflict-minimized subobjectives and activates them sequentially, temporally separating competing local influences. The interplay of switching and local interactions among variables, supplemented by structured correlated perturbations, gives rise to collective search behavior including coordinated cluster motion. Using this framework, we develop and test a solver for sparse Ising optimization. On G64, a large sparse instance with a highly heterogeneous degree distribution from the longstanding Gset Max-Cut benchmark suite, Cosm establishes a new best-known cut of 8753. On large random-graph instances G61 and G70, whose best-known cuts of 5799 and 9595 have been difficult for prior heuristics to attain, a vectorized CPU implementation of Cosm reliably reaches these cuts with times-to-target of 15 s and 2.4 s, respectively. Cosm also heuristically attains the certified optimum of G81, the largest Gset instance (a 20,000-variable two-dimensional spin glass), along with those of G72 and G77. Tests on planted-solution spin-glass benchmarks suggest more favorable empirical scaling than that previously reported for seven compared solvers. Cosm demonstrates that, from simple interacting elements and a new form of orchestration, effective search can emerge.

♻ ☆ Learning linear dynamical systems under convex constraints
Hemant Tyagi, Denis Efimov
We consider the problem of finite-time identification of linear dynamical systems from $T$ samples of a single trajectory. Recent results have predominantly focused on the setup where either no structural assumption is made on the system matrix $A^* \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$, or specific structural assumptions (e.g. sparsity) are made on $A^*$. We assume prior structural information on $A^*$ is available, which can be captured in the form of a convex set $\mathcal{K}$ containing $A^*$. For the solution of the ensuing constrained least squares estimator, we derive non-asymptotic error bounds in the Frobenius norm that depend on the local size of $\mathcal{K}$ at $A^*$. To illustrate the usefulness of these results, we instantiate them for four examples, namely when (i) $A^*$ is sparse and $\mathcal{K}$ is a suitably scaled $\ell_1$ ball; (ii) $\mathcal{K}$ is a subspace; (iii) $\mathcal{K}$ consists of matrices each of which is formed by sampling a bivariate convex function on a uniform $n \times n$ grid (convex regression); (iv) $\mathcal{K}$ consists of matrices each row of which is formed by uniform sampling (with step size $1/T$) of a univariate Lipschitz function. In all these situations, we show that $A^*$ can be reliably estimated for values of $T$ much smaller than what is needed for the unconstrained setting.

♻ ☆ Controllability of finite-dimensional linear fractional systems under uncertain parameters
Idriss Boutaayamou, Fouad Et-Tahri, Lahcen Maniar
This paper investigates the controllability of finite-dimensional linear fractional systems involving an uncertain parameter. We establish new results on the simultaneous and average controllability. In particular, we show that average controllability can be characterized by the so-called average Kalman rank condition and the average Gramian matrix. Moreover, using the average Gramian matrix, we design an open-loop control with minimal energy. These results can be seen as a natural generalization of the classical results known for systems with integer-order derivatives. Finally, numerical simulations are provided to robustly validate the theoretical findings, with a focus on the fractional Rössler system for a damping parameter following either a Gaussian or a uniform distribution.
♻ ☆ Fast Trainable Multilinear Bases for Image Compression
Shiwen An, Zhongyi Ni, Huanhai Zhou, Jin-Guo Liu
The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), and their block-wise variants underpin most deployed image and video codecs. Their effectiveness rests on three properties: their runtime is near-linear (up to a polylogarithmic factor) in the image size, they are exactly invertible, and they carry few to no parameters. We generalize these transforms to dataset-adaptive isometric multilinear bases that keep all three properties at the cost of a polylogarithmic number of parameters, by parameterizing each basis as an isometric tensor network, inspired by quantum many-body theory, and training one shared basis per image dataset with Riemannian optimization. Because the family contains the DFT and the DCT-IV (a variant of the DCT) as exact points, training can start from these transforms, and it improves on its starting point at the compression level it is trained for. We evaluate the bases on natural photographs and line drawings. On photographs, which the cosine basis already fits well, the best trained basis leads the DCT only under aggressive truncation. On Quick Draw line drawings, under a common codec at matched quality, the best trained basis stores each image in about 20% fewer bytes than the 8x8 block cosine transform of the Joint Photographic Experts Group (JPEG) format, not counting the one-off storage of the basis.
♻ ☆ Optimal and Self Selection of Service Type in a Queueing System where Long Service Postpones the Need for the Next Service
Refael Hassin, Jiesen Wang
We study a make-to-order system with a finite set of customers. Production is stochastic with a nonlinear dependence between the ordered quantity and the production rate. Customers may have to queue until their turn arrives, and therefore their order decisions interact. Specifically, while being served, customers are aware of the queue length and choose one of two order quantities (or service types). The time to the next replenishment (their activity time) is stochastic and depends on the order quantities. A customer is inactive during service and while waiting in the queue. We refer to the type of service with a greater ratio of expected activity to service time as ``more efficient''. In the centralized case, the system is interested in maximizing the steady-state average number of active customers, which is referred to as the efficiency of the system. We show that choosing the more efficient service is not always optimal, but the optimal strategy can be approximated well by selecting one of three threshold strategies which depend on the number of inactive customers. In the decentralized case, each customer acts to maximize the fraction of time she is active. We observe that individuals and the manager have opposite incentives: When the queue is long, individuals tend to choose the long service, while the manager prefers the short service in this case. This makes the system difficult to regulate. However, we show that simply removing the less efficient service significantly increases efficiency.

♻ ☆ Eigenvalue-Decomposition Cost Denoising for Predict-then-Optimize
Henry Aldridge-Krawciw, Irene Aldridge
Predict-then-optimize methods learn a mapping from features to unknown edge costs. They then solve the shortest-path problem on the predicted costs. We study a feature-free alternative for the case where the decision-maker observes many noisy cost vectors on a fixed network. The cost vectors are denoised by an eigenvalue decomposition (PCA) of their covariance matrix. Dijkstra's algorithm then runs on the result. We test this on the $5\times5$ grid of \citet{elmachtoub2022}, with $1000$ independent replications and a fresh ground truth in each. We compare against SPO+, against naive Dijkstra on noisy costs, and against two alternatives to a hand-picked rank $k$ (the Gavish-Donoho threshold and a Ledoit-Wolf filter). We also test a hybrid of SPO+ and PCA. Four findings emerge. First, the rank matters. Keeping $k=2$ components performs worse than no denoising. Second, when costs are close to linear in the features, the Gavish-Donoho threshold recovers the true rank without supervision. PCA-denoised Dijkstra outperforms SPO+ at $°=1$, but underperforms SPO+ at $°\geq 2$. The hybrid works best at $°=1$ and is slightly better than SPO+ at $°=2$. Third, when costs are strongly nonlinear ($°=4$), the signal is no longer low-rank, and only the Ledoit-Wolf filter clearly beats the naive baseline. Fourth, the benefit of denoising grows with network size on grids, but not on a layered non-grid network at high nonlinearity.

♻ ☆ Sparsity in control problems: Recent trends and open challenges
Luca Ballotta, Geethu Joseph, Waseem Abbas, Sophie M. Fosson, Chandra R. Murthy, Masaaki Nagahara, Alex Olshevsky, Kyle Poe, René Vidal
As in all fields of engineering, control engineers constantly face a dichotomy between achieving high performance and the limited availability of resources for sensing, actuation, and control. This tension often translates into formalizing design problems with sparsity constraints; that is, the design involves decision variables whose number, spatial reach, temporal spread, or other physical expressions are much smaller than in the ideal scenario of unconstrained optimization of a task-related performance metric. Even though this fundamental limitation underlines a plethora of methodological approaches and application domains, the control literature is fragmented into several lines of work tailored to specific scenarios. This survey fills the gap by bringing together several lines of work on handling sparsity in relevant control problems such as actuator scheduling, minimal-energy controllability, maximum hands-off control, and online convex optimization, and weaving a red thread through theoretical foundations and algorithms. Beyond establishing a coherent, structured narrative of problems and solutions for handling sparsity in control scenarios, we discuss open areas and relevant directions for future research, motivated by the growing complexity of control systems and their relations with key domains such as pervasive computing, distributed learning, cyberphysical security, and ecological footprint.

♻ ☆ Optimal Cuts and Optimal Faces of Exact Max-Cut Semidefinite Relaxations
Avinash Bhardwaj, Chen Chen, Vishnu Narayanan
An exact Max-Cut semidefinite relaxation can have optima outside the convex hull of optimal cut matrices. We study when this hull equals the optimal face and how to recognize equality. For rational weights, the unique optimal dual slack is recoverable in polynomial time, but its kernel may contain directions no optimal matrix uses. Under strict complementarity, recognition and recovery of all optimal cuts on equality instances take deterministic polynomial time. At dual rank one, this hypothesis is unnecessary. Recognition is polynomial-time Turing equivalent to exact rational semidefinite feasibility, even on simple unweighted graphs. Testing whether a supplied cut matrix is the unique optimum is many-one equivalent, even on connected simple graphs with a unique optimal cut. NP-completeness of recognition would imply NP equals coNP. Replication realizes doubly nonnegative matrices with positive diagonal and rational kernel as sign-spanned optimal dual slacks, preserving rank, complete positivity, and cp-rank.
♻ ☆ Modified Polyhedral Method to Elicit Shape-Free Utility and Reduction of Conservatism in Robust Optimization
Sainan Zhang, Shaoyan Guo, Melvyn Sim, Huifu Xu
In this paper, we propose a modified polyhedral method to elicit a decision maker's (DM's) nonlinear univariate utility function without explicit knowledge of its shape, Lipschitz modulus, or inflection point. Inspired by \cite{THS04} for linear multivariate utility elicitation, we extend the polyhedral method to the nonlinear setting by addressing two major challenges. First, we approximate the nonlinear utility function using a continuous piecewise linear function (PLF) represented by its increment vector, such that utility elicitation can be viewed as progressively reducing a polyhedral feasible region of increment vectors. Second, we iteratively shrink this polyhedron through hyperplane cuts generated from pairwise lottery comparisons. Since PLF approximation errors may cause the resulting hyperplanes to deviate from ideal cutting directions, we dynamically enrich the PLF by incorporating newly generated lottery outcomes as additional breakpoints. The elicited responses are then used to construct an ambiguity set of utility functions for decision making under worst-case expected utility. To mitigate the potential conservatism of the resulting maximin model, we use the analytic center of the ambiguity set as a nominal estimate of the DM's utility increment vector and derive, through dual reformulation, a flexible weighting scheme for controlling conservatism. The resulting model accommodates asymmetric bounds on utility increments around the analytic center and admits a single mixed-integer linear programming reformulation for piecewise linear utilities. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed elicitation method and conservatism-reduction approach. Finally, we discuss several potential extensions, including applications to multivariate nonlinear utility elicitation and dynamic pricing problems.
♻ ☆ Bilinear Mamba-Koopman Neural MPC for Varying Dynamics
Matan Pagi, Zohar Sorek
Koopman-based neural MPC models generate time-varying dynamics from historical data, but preserve convexity by enforcing that the system operator is independent of the current control input. This conditional independence constraint limits adaptation to changing dynamics within a single MPC horizon, particularly under time-varying conditions and under stale-plan execution. We propose Bilinear Mamba-Koopman Neural MPC, a minimal extension that introduces control-dependent coupling in the latent dynamics, allowing the effective operator to adapt to the current input. The resulting model is a strict generalization of the standard linear, conditional-independence formulation, adds less than 1% parameters through a low-rank structure, and admits exact model Jacobians that enable efficient Sequential Convex Programming (SCP) with monotone-descent and KKT convergence results under standard trust-region assumptions. Across CartPole and RSCP benchmarks in time-invariant and time-varying regimes, the proposed model matches or improves forecasting accuracy on every cell when training noise is averaged out, with strict gains where control-state coupling is structurally present. Its main closed-loop gains appear in the RSCP TV task, where iterative SCP improves adaptation within the horizon and substantially stabilizes training; in CartPole TV, the gains are modest but consistent. In delayed re-planning experiments on the time-varying variants, the bilinear model degrades more gracefully under stale-plan execution, maintaining a consistent advantage on CartPole TV and a substantially larger robustness margin on RSCP TV. These results show that control-dependent latent dynamics provide a simple and effective mechanism for robust MPC under varying conditions.

☆ Non-Euclidean Gradient Descent Has Many Edges of Stability
Peter Zaika, Zakhar Shumaylov
Recent observations that deep learning models train at the edge of stability have renewed interest in understanding stability properties of classical optimization algorithms. For quadratic objectives, standard gradient descent has a sharp stability threshold: it converges from every initialization when $η<2/L$, diverges from almost every initialization when $η>2/L$, and diverges from every nonzero initialization when $η>2/μ$. For non-Euclidean gradient descent, the corresponding known guarantees are weaker: convergence holds for every initialization when $η<2/S$, where $S$ is the generalized sharpness, while every nonzero initialization diverges when $η>2/μ$. The behavior in the intermediate regime $2/S<η<2/μ$ is not fully characterized. We show that Hilbertian norms are the only ones for which $2/S$ is an almost-everywhere sharp threshold for every positive-definite quadratic objective. Using linear conjugacy between non-Euclidean and Euclidean gradient descent, we show that for general norms the intermediate regime can contain arbitrarily many edges of stability associated with distinct attracting directions. We identify a forward-invariant region of exponentially divergent directions beyond the generalized stability threshold. When the directions of minimum curvature are finite and nondegenerate, we prove that, sufficiently close to $2/μ$ from below, only their invariant directions remain convergent. We give smooth two-dimensional constructions with arbitrarily many distinct thresholds, arbitrarily large relative threshold separation and show these properties to be stable.
☆ An adaptive Galerkin neural-network method for minimum-norm control of wave equations
Nguyen Gia Hien
We develop an adaptive Galerkin neural-network method for computing minimum-$L^2$-norm interior controls for wave equations with spatially varying coefficients. Within the Hilbert Uniqueness Method, adjoint waves are approximated directly in space-time by least-squares Galerkin projections onto trial spaces enriched by neural-network basis functions selected through residual-based training. Linear Galerkin solves determine the adjoint approximations, and a separate linear system reconstructs the control. The least-squares objective provides an indicator for adaptive enrichment and stopping; the experiments use a Ritz-based terminal-data version whose continuous-error interpretation additionally requires an eigenpair consistency estimate. The main difficulty is that adjoint errors perturb this reconstruction system. Assuming observability of the continuous equation, we derive sufficient stability conditions involving a worst-case factor $\sqrt{n}$ multiplying the maximal adjoint error, where $n$ is the number of retained terminal modes. A fully discrete error estimate separates terminal-space truncation, adjoint approximation, and assembly errors, yielding convergence to the minimum-norm control when the truncation error, the $\sqrt{n}$-weighted adjoint error, and the assembly errors tend to zero as $n$ grows. For spectral terminal bases, additional regularity and uniform contraction assumptions yield quantitative convergence rates and show that $O(\log n)$ accepted enrichment steps per mode suffice to balance the neural and truncation errors. Numerical experiments on a nonconvex Cassini oval, a square containing a low-speed lens, and a three-dimensional ball with a graded coefficient illustrate the method.

Yuriy Dorn, Osman Osmanov, Timofei Loginov, Nazarii Tupitsa, Darina Dvinskikh, Alexander Gasnikov
We study stochastic convex optimization, where each sampled function can be evaluated at two arbitrary points. Our accelerated method chooses step sizes, batch sizes and smoothing radii from function values. A forward difference between smoothing scales controls the radius; we account for changes in the smoothed objective. Under the stated regularity and second-moment assumptions, exact function evaluations give \begin{multline*} \mathbb{E}\bigl[f(x_N)-f(x^\star)\bigr] \le \widetilde{O}\biggl( \frac{\sqrt{d}\,M_2 D}{\sqrt{T}} +\min\biggl( \frac{L D^2}{N^2},\; \frac{d^{1/4} M D}{N}+\frac{\sqrt{d}\,M D^2}{γ_{\max} N^2} \biggr)\biggr). \end{multline*} Here $N,T,d,D$ denote the numbers of optimization steps and paired evaluations, the dimension and a feasible-set diameter bound, respectively. Evaluations are available within Euclidean distance $γ_{\max}$ of the feasible set. For the population objective $f(x)=\mathbb{E}_ξ F(x,ξ)$, $M$ satisfies $|f(x)-f(y)|\le M\|x-y\|_2$, and $M_2$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}_ξ\|\nabla F(x,ξ)\|_2^2\le M_2^2$ for sample weak gradients in the interior of the evaluation domain. The method requires no $L,M,M_2$, where $L$ is a Lipschitz constant of $\nabla f$; set $L=+\infty$ without smoothness. The method uses exactly $2T$ values in $3N$ sequential sampling rounds with predetermined batches, or $5N$ with batches chosen from observations. An extension selects a search radius without a supplied distance bound. Fixed radius parameters can leave nonvanishing error; suitable choices depending on the budgets yield convergence.

We study Nesterov's accelerated gradient method with its standard constant parameters for smooth strongly convex optimization. To this end, we construct candidate worst-case trajectories by combining planar spirals with a common contraction factor that satisfy a self-similarity condition. Each component rotates by a fixed angle at every iteration. The exact factor is the optimal value of a linear optimization problem over probability measures on a fixed disk, with constraints derived from smooth strongly convex interpolation. Every optimal measure has a common contraction factor, which is also the largest factor for which the angular interpolation conditions are feasible. We also show that this worst-case asymptotic rate can be realized by a \emph{single} function in a finite-dimensional space whose iterates attain this factor. A matching upper bound holds uniformly over all functions in the class and all finite dimensions. Consequently, allowing the function, dimension, and initial point to vary with the iteration horizon does not increase the worst-case asymptotic factor. We also show that the exact factor is $1-4/(3\sqrtκ)+o(κ^{-1/2})$ as $κ\to\infty$, where $κ=L/μ$ is the ratio of the gradient Lipschitz constant to the strong convexity parameter.

Vladimir Kirill Bickov, Neil Yorke-Smith
Latent recursion repeatedly processes internal representations through the same neural network. Recent work has shown this approach to be effective on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and maze solving. However, whether latent recursion can support neural routing remains unclear. We introduce RELAGRAM (Recursive Latent Graph Model), a novel approach that brings latent recursion to graph combinatorial optimization. RELAGRAM encodes a capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) instance as edge tokens; a compact transformer recurrently updates the latent representations of these tokens. On CVRP-100 instances, the 0.53M-parameter RELAGRAM achieves gaps to a PyVRP reference of 13.4%, 9.8%, and 8.3% under greedy decoding, eightfold symmetry augmentation, and 256-candidate search, respectively. Trained only on CVRP-100, RELAGRAM generalizes zero-shot to CVRP-500 and CVRP-1000, achieving gaps of 15.6% and 21.7% under 256-candidate search. Together, these results demonstrate that latent recursion is a promising approach to neural routing.

☆ On the minimizer of the barycentric isoperimetric ratio among connected planar sets
Chiara Gambicchia, Aldo Pratelli, Clara Torres-Latorre
Among connected, planar sets, the ratio between the isoperimetric deficit and the squared barycentric asymmetry is known to be bounded from below by a strictly positive constant (as proved in recent papers by Bianchini-Croce-Henrot and Gambicchia-Pratelli). This opens the natural question whether the infimum is attained at some set. In this paper, we prove that a minimizer for this ratio actually exists, and moreover it is simply connected.

☆ Duality Theory for Filter Stability in Hidden Markov Models
Prashant G. Mehta
This article is concerned with the problem of nonlinear (stochastic) filter stability for a discrete time hidden Markov model (HMM) with finite state and observation spaces. For this purpose, a comprehensive duality theory is developed whereby the dual control system is a backward stochastic difference equation (BSDE). The duality is expressed in two inter-related forms. In its variational form, the minimum mean squared error of optimal filtering equals the value of a dual optimal control problem. In its structural form, controllability (resp. stabilizability) of the BSDE and observability (resp. detectability) of the HMM are dual properties. The dual optimal control problem supplies the Lyapunov function and the dissipation: the former is the value function (a variance), the latter the optimal running cost accumulated over the horizon. The main result is an invariance principle: under any one of three model properties---ergodicity of the Markov matrix, or observability or detectability of the HMM---zero dissipation over a finite horizon forces the Lyapunov function to vanish. A converse is also obtained: detectability is necessary. Two applications are given. The first is filter stability in chi-squared divergence: the invariance principle is applied in the manner of LaSalle, to limits of trajectories along which the dissipation vanishes asymptotically, the role of the model properties being to render the zero-dissipation set trivial. The second is a quantitative form of the invariance principle, through a Poincare constant, from which convergence rates follow. Both the model properties that govern stability and the Lyapunov function that certifies it are thus obtained from a dual optimal control problem, as in the classical theory for the linear Gaussian model.
☆ Multilevel Monte Carlo for Zeroth-Order Stochastic Bilevel Optimization with Inexact Lower Level Solves
Neil K. Chada, Mohammad S. Salehi, Mathias Staudigl, Simon Weissmann
Variational regularization techniques are dominant in the field of mathematical imaging. The expressiveness of these methods heavily depends on the adopted regularization formulation which usually involves a number of parameters which have to be fine-tuned by the user. To circumvent the heavy computational costs associated with this parameter tuning, data-driven learning strategies have turned out to be a useful strategy. Selecting parameters by learning from data gives rise to a hierarchical (bilevel) optimization problem, which is in general computationally hard to solve. Our aim in this paper is to develop a data-efficient solution strategy for the bilevel learning problem. To that end, we propose a multilevel Monte Carlo derivative-free optimization method that couples Gaussian smoothing of the upper-level objective (parameter selection) with a hierarchy of lower-level (variational regularization) solution accuracies. Being agnostic towards the specific way the lower-level problem is solved, we derive explicit oracle complexity and computational cost statements for approximately solving the entire bilevel learning problem. Our statements are parameterized by the employed lower-level solution method, thus allowing for a direct cost accounting from the variational reconstruction method to the parameter selection problem. This enables us to give a universal end-to-end complexity analysis of bilevel learning, valid for the most important optimization routines in inverse problems, rather than for a specific choice of methods.

☆ Training-Free Multi-Agent Cooperative Embodied Search from Uncertain Vision-Language Priors
Fan Pu, Keshu Wu, Jiwan Jiang, Shiyu Shen, Zhiwen Fan, Zhengzhong Tu, Jiachen Li, Yang Zhou
Real-world Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to act under partial observability, where map structure, semantic cues, and target locations may be incomplete or incorrectly inferred by foundation models. This paper presents a lightweight, training-free, and uncertainty-aware framework for cooperative multi-agent multi-target search in mapless environments. Instead of learning an end-to-end navigation policy, the framework separates high-level semantic reasoning from low-level execution through a scalable graph-optimization backbone. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) serve only as hypothesis generators, proposing semantic zones, target-location cues, and possible navigable connections. These outputs are treated as uncertain priors and further refined using online observations and graph-context evidence. Cooperative navigation is then formulated as a rolling-horizon multi-agent mixed-integer linear program with a lexicographic objective that first maximizes target-directed reward and then reduces travel distance, uncertain-edge use, and repeated visits. Experiments derived from 100 Matterport3D test cases show that the proposed framework improves target coverage and search efficiency over representative baseline methods, while shared information and joint planning enable more balanced workloads across agents. By operating on an abstract graph without relying on embodiment-specific policy parameters, the framework scales across varying numbers of agents and targets, generalizes to unseen environments, and accommodates different perception modules and low-level controllers without task-specific retraining.

For the ambiguity sets constructed by the $φ$-divergence and the Wasserstein distance, we build the tractable reformulations for the DRO models. We conduct numerical experiments to test the asymptotic properties for the estimation. We also conduct experiments to illustrate that the asymptotic normality might not hold when the fourth moments of the returns do not exist.

We study a Truck-as-Hub Vehicle Routing Problem with Drones in Rural Areas, in which multiple trucks each carry a dedicated fleet of drones.
